title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) is a common endocrine disorder caused by autonomous parathyroid hormone secretion, leading to hypercalcemia and systemic complications involving bone, kidney, and neurocognitive function. This activity reviews the etiology, epidemiology, pathophysiology, and the varying clinical presentations of PHPT. Most cases arise from a single benign adenoma, with less frequent multigland disease or carcinoma. Widespread biochemical screening has shifted the most frequent presentation from classic symptomatic disease to predominantly asymptomatic hypercalcemia, including normocalcemic and normohormonal variants.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Introduction
content: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) is an endocrine disorder defined by autonomous overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH), resulting in hypercalcemia and disrupted calcium homeostasis. The most common etiology is a single benign adenoma, while multigland hyperplasia, multiple adenomas, and parathyroid carcinoma are less frequent. [1] Variants, eg, normocalcemic and normohormonal PHPT, represent milder biochemical manifestations of the same disease process. PHPT is the leading cause of hypercalcemia in the outpatient setting, predominantly affecting postmenopausal women. The incidence of PHPT is rising due to increased routine biochemical screening. The underlying pathophysiology involves a shift in the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) set point, causing persistent PTH secretion despite elevated serum calcium. This leads to increased bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, and intestinal calcium absorption. [2] [3]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Introduction
content: Histopathologically, parathyroid adenomas are well-circumscribed lesions composed primarily of chief cells with reduced stromal fat. Hyperplasia is characterized by diffuse enlargement of all 4 glands, whereas carcinoma is identified by capsular or vascular invasion. The clinical presentation has shifted from classic symptomatic disease, such as nephrolithiasis, bone pain, and fractures, to predominantly asymptomatic hypercalcemia detected incidentally. Diagnostic evaluation relies exclusively on biochemical testing, focusing on confirming elevated or inappropriately elevated PTH in the presence of hypercalcemia after secondary causes have been excluded. Imaging studies for localization are reserved solely for surgical planning.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Introduction
content: Parathyroidectomy remains the only curative treatment, with cure rates exceeding 95%. Medical management and observation are suitable for selected patients who are asymptomatic or considered poor surgical candidates. Prognosis is excellent with timely surgical intervention, as both bone density and renal function typically improve, and recurrence is rare. Patients managed conservatively often remain stable for years with appropriate monitoring. Untreated PHPT can result in complications, eg, osteoporosis, nephrolithiasis, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and cardiovascular changes. Surgical complications, including transient hypocalcemia, hungry bone syndrome, or recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, are uncommon and generally manageable by experienced clinicians. [4] [5]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Etiology -- Classic Primary Hyperparathyroidism
content: PHPT is characterized by autonomous overproduction of PTH that occurs independently of normal calcium feedback regulation, leading to hypercalcemia. The disorder arises from clonal dysregulation and overgrowth of parathyroid tissue, most commonly involving a single gland. Reduced expression or altered function of the CaSR contributes to this loss of calcium-mediated inhibition.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Etiology -- Classic Primary Hyperparathyroidism
content: Under normal physiology, activation of the CaSR on parathyroid chief cells suppresses PTH secretion, PTH gene expression, and cellular proliferation. In PHPT, the set point for calcium-induced inhibition of PTH release is shifted upward, resulting in higher circulating calcium levels required to suppress PTH secretion. PTH hypersecretion subsequently promotes bone resorption, renal tubular calcium reabsorption, and increased intestinal calcium absorption via enhanced renal production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, while simultaneously reducing renal phosphate reabsorption. [6] PHPT ranks as the third most prevalent endocrine disorder, following diabetes mellitus and thyroid disease. The etiological distribution is as follows: Single parathyroid adenoma: 80% to 85% Multigland disease (hyperplasia or multiple adenomas): 10% to 15% Parathyroid carcinoma: <1%

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Etiology -- Classic Primary Hyperparathyroidism
content: Atypical parathyroid adenomas exhibit histologic features suggestive of malignancy but lack evidence of invasive growth and are therefore classified within the benign disease spectrum. Multigland disease occurs more frequently in hereditary syndromes, eg, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1), multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN2A), and CDC73 -related disorders, as well as in lithium-associated PHPT. (Please refer to the Differential Diagnosis section for more information.) Although most adenomas arise in orthotopic parathyroid glands, up to 10% are found in ectopic locations. Common ectopic sites include the thymus, thyroid gland, pericardium, retroesophageal space, and superior mediastinum. Rare sites comprise the pharynx, lateral neck, and esophagus. [7] [8] [1] [9] [10] [11]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Etiology -- Normocalcemic Primary Hyperparathyroidism
content: Normocalcemic primary hyperparathyroidism (NPHPT) is a variant of primary hyperparathyroidism defined by persistently elevated PTH levels with normal total and ionized serum calcium concentrations, confirmed by repeated measurements over at least 3 months. This disorder results from autonomous parathyroid overactivity, most often due to a single adenoma or, less frequently, multigland hyperplasia, but without sufficient PTH excess to induce overt hypercalcemia.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Etiology -- Normocalcemic Primary Hyperparathyroidism
content: The underlying pathophysiology mirrors that of classical hypercalcemic PHPT, involving clonal dysregulation of parathyroid cells and reduced CaSR expression. While many patients are asymptomatic, some may present with nephrolithiasis or osteoporosis. The clinical course is variable, and only a minority of cases progress to hypercalcemia over several years. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Normocalcemic Hyperparathyroidism ," for further information. [12] [13]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Etiology -- Normohormonal Primary Hyperparathyroidism
content: Normohormonal primary hyperparathyroidism (NH-PHPT) is defined by elevated serum calcium levels with PTH concentrations that remain within the normal reference range. NH-PHPT results from autonomous parathyroid overactivity, most frequently due to a single adenoma, although multigland disease is more common in this variant than in classic hyperparathyroidism. PTH levels are described as “inappropriately normal” because they do not suppress in response to hypercalcemia. The pathophysiology of NH-PHPT is similar to that of classical PHPT, involving clonal proliferation of parathyroid cells and altered CaSR responsiveness, which leads to impaired calcium-mediated feedback inhibition. Patients typically exhibit milder biochemical abnormalities but may still develop osteoporosis, nephrolithiasis, or other end-organ complications. [14]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Epidemiology
content: PHPT represents the most common identifiable cause of hypercalcemia in ambulatory patients, particularly among postmenopausal women. [1] The female-to-male ratio is approximately 3:1 to 4:1, with peak incidence occurring between ages 50 and 60. [15] In the United States, the age-adjusted prevalence is estimated at 233 per 100,000 women and 85 per 100,000 men. Incidence rates are higher among Black individuals compared to White populations, and lower among Asians and Hispanics. [16] [7]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Epidemiology
content: The widespread adoption of automated biochemical screening and routine serum calcium testing has shifted the clinical profile of PHPT from predominantly symptomatic presentations, such as nephrolithiasis, osteitis fibrosa cystica, and bone pain, to mainly asymptomatic or mild hypercalcemic forms. In regions with limited laboratory screening and less frequent vitamin D repletion, PHPT continues to present as symptomatic disease with skeletal or renal complications. The normocalcemic variant of PHPT has become increasingly recognized as PTH assays are more frequently utilized during evaluations for osteoporosis or nephrolithiasis. [6]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Pathophysiology
content: PTH, produced by the chief cells of the parathyroid glands, regulates extracellular calcium homeostasis through feedback mechanisms mediated by the CaSR. A decrease in serum ionized calcium reduces CaSR activity, which stimulates PTH secretion. PTH subsequently increases bone resorption, enhances distal tubular calcium reabsorption, and activates renal 1-α-hydroxylase, thereby promoting intestinal calcium absorption via 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. [17] [18] [7] [8]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Pathophysiology
content: In primary hyperparathyroidism, clonal overactivity of parathyroid tissue elevates the set-point for calcium-mediated inhibition, resulting in persistent PTH secretion despite hypercalcemia. The typical biochemical profile includes elevated serum calcium, low or low-normal serum phosphate, and variable hypercalciuria due to increased filtered calcium load exceeding tubular reabsorption capacity. [6]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Histopathology
content: PHPT most commonly presents as a solitary parathyroid adenoma, typically well-circumscribed, soft, and encapsulated, and usually weighing less than 1 g. Grossly, these adenomas are reddish-brown or tan, exhibit a smooth surface, and display a thin rim of compressed normal parathyroid tissue at the periphery. Multiglandular hyperplasia, involving all 4 glands, is less common and manifests as diffusely enlarged, nonencapsulated glands. Although rare, parathyroid carcinoma is generally larger, firm, gray-white, and adherent to adjacent structures.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Histopathology
content: Microscopically, parathyroid adenomas are primarily composed of chief cells arranged in solid, trabecular, or acinar patterns, with a significant reduction in stromal fat relative to normal glands. Oxyphil cell adenomas are rare but can occur. Chronic excess of PTH results in osteoclastic bone resorption, cortical thinning, fibrosis, and cystic degeneration. In advanced cases, osteitis fibrosa cystica may develop, which is characterized by fibroblast proliferation, multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells, and brown hemosiderin deposits, known as “brown tumors.” [19]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Histopathology
content: Parathyroid carcinoma is histologically defined by capsular, vascular, or perineural invasion, a trabecular growth pattern, and increased mitotic activity. These features are often accompanied by dense fibrous bands that separate tumor lobules. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Parathyroid Cancer ," for further information. [20]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- History and Physical
content: Historically, primary hyperparathyroidism was most often diagnosed in patients presenting with nephrolithiasis, osteoporosis, or pathologic fractures. Since the 1970s, the widespread adoption of automated serum chemistry panels has shifted detection toward asymptomatic disease, with most cases now identified through incidental findings of hypercalcemia. [21] Diagnosis currently relies on biochemical confirmation, demonstrated by elevated or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone levels in the presence of hypercalcemia.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- History and Physical -- Clinical History
content: During medical history assessment, clinicians should evaluate for renal calculi, bone pain, myalgias or muscle weakness, neurocognitive symptoms (eg, fatigue, memory changes, or depression), gastrointestinal discomfort, and medication use, including thiazide diuretics, lithium, calcium supplements, vitamin B supplements, and vitamin D preparations. Despite the absence of overt symptoms in many patients, up to 55% demonstrate subclinical nephrocalcinosis or nonobstructing renal stones. Among symptomatic patients, up to 75% present with acute renal colic or nephrolithiasis. [22] [23] [24]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Physical examination findings are frequently unremarkable, but should emphasize identifying complications related to hypercalcemia or alternative etiologies. Palpable parathyroid masses occur infrequently; however, a firm, fixed cervical mass in the setting of hypercalcemia warrants concern for parathyroid carcinoma. Associated manifestations of hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia include bone or joint pain, fractures, osteoporosis, muscle weakness, fatigue, abdominal pain, anorexia, constipation, depression, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbance, hypertension, cardiac arrhythmias, left ventricular hypertrophy, nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, and polyuria.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Evaluation
content: Patients presenting with clinical features or diagnostic findings of hypercalcemia should undergo evaluation for PHPT through laboratory testing (see Table 1 ). Diagnosis is confirmed when elevated serum calcium (total or ionized) coincides with an inappropriately high or normal PTH level measured simultaneously. Hypercalcemia is defined as total calcium greater than 10.2 mg/dL (2.55 mmol/L) or ionized calcium greater than 5.6 mg/dL (1.40 mmol/L).

content: The reference range for intact PTH varies by assay but is generally 10 to 65 pg/mL (1.1–6.9 pmol/L). As approximately half of serum calcium is protein-bound, total calcium should be corrected for albumin (corrected calcium = measured calcium + 0.8 × [4 – albumin]). Direct measurement of ionized calcium is preferred when albumin levels are abnormal or total calcium is borderline. In PHPT, serum phosphorus is usually low or low-normal due to PTH's phosphaturic action. title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Evaluation -- Skeletal and Renal Imaging
content: Skeletal and renal assessments are not required for diagnosis but may provide valuable adjunctive information. Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) should be performed at the lumbar spine, hip, and distal one-third radius to evaluate bone mineral density (BMD). Imaging for vertebral fractures, eg, vertebral fracture assessment or plain x-rays, may also be indicated. Renal evaluation includes 24-hour urinary calcium measurement and renal imaging, eg, ultrasound, noncontrast computed tomography (CT), or KUB x-ray, to screen for nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis, which may be clinically silent in up to 20% of patients. [6]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Evaluation -- Localizing Imaging
content: Localization imaging is not necessary for diagnosis, but is essential for preoperative planning and should be ordered by the operating surgeon. High-resolution neck ultrasonography and technetium-99m sestamibi scans, often combined with single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), are standard first-line modalities. If these studies are inconclusive, 4-dimensional CT or F-18 fluorocholine positron emission tomography (PET)/CT may be utilized for greater sensitivity, particularly in cases of ectopic or multigland disease. Selective venous sampling is reserved for complex or reoperative cases. [28] [29] [30] [31] [32] Additional information on localizing imaging techniques is provided below under surgical management.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Evaluation -- Preoperative and Perioperative Evaluation
content: Laryngoscopy is recommended both before and after surgery to evaluate the function of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, particularly in reoperative cases or when voice changes are present. Baseline serum calcium and PTH levels should be measured on the day of surgery for comparison with intraoperative values. Vitamin D deficiency should be corrected preoperatively to reduce the risk of postoperative hypocalcemia or hungry bone syndrome.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Evaluation -- Normocalcemic Primary Hyperparathyroidism
content: NPHPT is characterized by persistently elevated PTH levels with normal calcium concentrations. Diagnosis requires exclusion of all secondary causes of hyperparathyroidism, such as vitamin D deficiency, renal insufficiency (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²), calcium or magnesium deficiency, malabsorption, hypercalciuria, and specific medications (bisphosphonates, denosumab, lithium, proton pump inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors). [12]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Evaluation -- Normohormonal Primary Hyperparathyroidism
content: In NH-PHPT, patients have hypercalcemia with PTH values within the laboratory reference range. In this presentation, PTH is inappropriately normal given the degree of hypercalcemia. Evaluation follows the same principles as classic PHPT: confirm persistent hypercalcemia, rule out secondary causes (eg, medications, malignancy, vitamin D intoxication, or granulomatous disease), and assess renal and skeletal involvement. [14]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Evaluation -- Parathyroid Crisis
content: Bone turnover markers and neurocognitive testing are not routinely recommended. However, when PHPT presents with severe or symptomatic hypercalcemia (>14 mg/dL), urgent evaluation for parathyroid crisis is necessary. Such cases often warrant inpatient management, aggressive medical therapy, and early surgical consultation. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Resistant Hypercalcemia ," for further information. [33]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Treatment / Management
content: Surgical intervention remains the sole definitive treatment for PHPT and is recommended for all eligible patients, irrespective of age or symptomatology, once diagnostic criteria are fulfilled. Parathyroidectomy achieves cure rates above 95% in experienced centers and improves bone mineral density, renal function, and overall quality of life. Observation and medical management are reserved for asymptomatic individuals, those with mild biochemical abnormalities, or patients deemed unsuitable for surgery due to comorbidities or elevated anesthesia risk (see Table 3 ). [6] [34] [35]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Treatment / Management -- Indications for surgery
content: Surgical intervention is indicated for all symptomatic patients, including those presenting with nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, fragility fractures, or osteoporosis. Additionally, surgery may be considered for individuals exhibiting neurocognitive or neuropsychiatric symptoms attributable to PHPT, as well as for those who prefer definitive management. Asymptomatic patients who meet any of the following criteria are also eligible for parathyroidectomy: Age <50 years Serum calcium >1.0 mg/dL (0.25 mmol/L) above the upper limit of normal Creatinine clearance <60 mL/min or eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² Bone mineral density T-score ≤–2.5 at any site (eg, lumbar spine, hip, or distal radius) Presence of vertebral fracture on imaging Renal stones or calcifications on ultrasound or CT Hypercalciuria (>250 mg/24 hours in women and >300 mg/24 hours in men)

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Treatment / Management -- Preoperative localization
content: Neck ultrasonography: High-resolution neck ultrasound provides anatomical visualization of the parathyroid glands and is widely available. The sensitivity of ultrasound for identifying abnormal parathyroid glands typically ranges from 70% to 81%, with specificity between 90% and 95%. Sensitivity is reduced in cases of multiglandular disease, small adenomas, posteriorly located glands, or ectopic mediastinal lesions. Ultrasound is also operator-dependent, yields no functional information, and is less reliable for ectopic, mediastinal, or posteriorly situated glands. [31] [36] [3]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Treatment / Management -- Preoperative localization
content: Technetium-99m sestamibi (MIBI) scintigraphy: MIBI scans (planar scintigraphy or SPECT/CT) assess enriched mitochondrial activity in hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue, giving functional information. Reported sensitivity ranges from 64% to 91%, depending on the imaging protocol, gland size, and presence of multigland disease, while specificity ranges from 83% to 96%. Planar MIBI imaging alone has lower sensitivity (approximately 42%–79%). SPECT/CT, which combines functional and anatomic imaging, significantly improves localization, achieving sensitivities up to 97% and high specificity. Sensitivity is reduced in multiglandular hyperplasia, small (<500 mg) adenomas, and cystic or normohormonal disease variants. When combined with neck ultrasound, the sensitivity for localization exceeds 90%, and in high-volume centers can reach as high as 96%, with specificity between 83% and 94%. [31] [36] [3]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Treatment / Management -- Intraoperative PTH monitoring
content: Intraoperative PTH monitoring provides biochemical confirmation of surgical success and reduces the risk of persistent or recurrent disease. PTH has a half-life of 3 to 5 minutes. Therefore, a 50% or greater reduction from baseline within 10 to 20 minutes after gland excision indicates successful removal of all hypersecreting tissue. A final PTH value falling into the normal range further supports biochemical cure. If the expected drop does not occur, exploration continues to identify additional hyperfunctioning glands. Routine intraoperative PTH monitoring is particularly useful in minimally invasive and reoperative surgeries, as it allows real-time decision-making and minimizes unnecessary dissection. [34] [35]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Treatment / Management -- Minimally invasive parathyroidectomy
content: Minimally invasive parathyroidectomy (MIP) is the preferred surgical approach when preoperative imaging localizes a single adenoma. The technique uses a small incision (2–3 cm) and is explicitly directed at the abnormal gland, allowing less tissue dissection, reduced operative time, a shorter hospital stay, and a faster recovery. MIP may be performed under local, regional, or general anesthesia, depending on the patient's and surgeon's preference. Intraoperative PTH monitoring (see below) enhances success rates and confirms cure in real time. Conversion to bilateral exploration may be required if intraoperative findings suggest multiglandular disease or if intraoperative PTH levels fail to fall appropriately.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Treatment / Management -- Bilateral neck exploration
content: Bilateral neck exploration remains the gold standard for cases where localization studies are negative, inconclusive, or suggest multiglandular hyperplasia. Bilateral neck exploration is also indicated in patients with familial syndromes (eg, MEN1, MEN2A) or lithium-associated PHPT, which are associated with multigland disease. During bilateral neck exploration, all 4 parathyroid glands are identified and evaluated for enlargement or nodularity with the goal of excising all hyperfunctioning tissue while preserving at least 1 viable normal gland to prevent permanent hypoparathyroidism. Although bilateral neck exploration is more extensive than MIP, it remains a safe and curative option in experienced hands. [34] [35]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Treatment / Management -- Special surgical considerations
content: Special consideration is required in the following clinical settings: Pregnancy : Parathyroidectomy can be performed safely in the second trimester when medically indicated. Reoperative surgery : Should be performed only by experienced endocrine surgeons and requires positive preoperative localization. Parathyroid carcinoma : En bloc resection with ipsilateral thyroid lobectomy and surrounding soft tissue is required to achieve negative margins. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Parathyroid Cancer ," for further information. [20]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Treatment / Management -- Postoperative Considerations
content: Postoperative care includes monitoring for hypocalcemia and hungry bone syndrome. Hungry bone syndrome occurs in up to 10% of cases, particularly after long-standing disease or severe hypercalcemia. Management includes high-dose oral or IV calcium and active vitamin D (calcitriol) replacement. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Hungry Bone Syndrome ," for further information. [39] Transient hypocalcemia occurs in approximately 50% of patients and should be managed with supplementation as needed.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Treatment / Management -- Medical Management and Surveillance
content: For patients with PHPT who are not surgical candidates or who elect nonoperative management, the primary goals are to control hypercalcemia, preserve bone density, and monitor for renal complications. Calcium intake should be maintained within the normal dietary range (1,000–1,200 mg/day) to prevent secondary PTH stimulation. Vitamin D deficiency should be corrected to achieve a 25-hydroxyvitamin D level >30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L), which can reduce PTH levels and mitigate bone loss. Cinacalcet, a calcimimetic that activates the calcium-sensing receptor, effectively lowers serum calcium in over 70% of patients but has minimal effect on BMD. Bisphosphonates (eg, alendronate) and denosumab can increase BMD, particularly at cortical sites, but do not normalize calcium. When both hypercalcemia and osteoporosis coexist, combination therapy with cinacalcet and an antiresorptive agent is appropriate. [40] [41]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Treatment / Management -- Medical Management and Surveillance
content: Patients managed medically require regular surveillance, including annual serum calcium, creatinine, or eGFR, and vitamin D testing. PTH should be repeated as clinically indicated. DXA scans of the lumbar spine, hip, and distal radius every 1 to 2 years should be used to monitor osteoporosis. Renal imaging or 24-hour urinary calcium should be obtained if nephrolithiasis is suspected. Surgery should be reconsidered if the patient develops symptoms, worsening hypercalcemia (>1 mg/dL above normal), nephrolithiasis, significant bone loss (T-score ≤ –2.5), or declining renal function.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of PHPT includes numerous disorders characterized by hypercalcemia or elevated PTH levels. Accurate diagnosis relies on a comprehensive biochemical evaluation to differentiate PTH-dependent from PTH-independent causes of hypercalcemia.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Differential Diagnosis -- Secondary and Tertiary Hyperparathyroidism
content: Secondary hyperparathyroidism arises as a compensatory mechanism in response to chronic hypocalcemia or vitamin D deficiency. Common etiologies include chronic kidney disease (CKD), vitamin D deficiency, and malabsorption syndromes. In secondary hyperparathyroidism, calcium levels are low or normal, PTH is elevated, and phosphate is elevated in CKD or decreased in vitamin D deficiency. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Secondary Hyperparathyroidism ," for further information. [42]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Differential Diagnosis -- Secondary and Tertiary Hyperparathyroidism
content: Tertiary hyperparathyroidism develops following extended secondary hyperparathyroidism, particularly in patients undergoing dialysis, when parathyroid glands begin to secrete PTH autonomously. This condition leads to hypercalcemia and multiglandular hyperplasia. The simultaneous presence of elevated PTH and hypercalcemia distinguishes tertiary hyperparathyroidism from secondary hyperparathyroidism (elevated PTH, low or normal calcium) and from primary hyperparathyroidism (elevated PTH, hypercalcemia, but without preceding renal disease). [3]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Differential Diagnosis -- Normocalcemic Primary Hyperparathyroidism
content: NPHPT is defined by persistently elevated PTH with normal total and ionized calcium levels, confirmed on repeated measurements. Diagnosis requires exclusion of all secondary causes, eg, vitamin D deficiency, renal insufficiency, inadequate calcium intake, hypercalciuria, magnesium deficiency, or medication effects. Patients may present with subtle skeletal or renal manifestations. Longitudinal studies demonstrate that up to 20% of cases progress to classical hypercalcemic PHPT. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Normocalcemic Hyperparathyroidism ," for further information. [12]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Differential Diagnosis -- Normohormonal Primary Hyperparathyroidism
content: NH-PHPT is characterized by biochemical hypercalcemia with PTH levels that remain within the normal range but are inappropriately unsuppressed in the context of elevated calcium. In nonparathyroid causes of hypercalcemia, PTH is typically suppressed. Patients often present with single-gland disease, although the incidence of multiglandular involvement is higher than in classic PHPT. Intraoperative assessment frequently requires bilateral neck exploration, and preoperative localization is less sensitive. Despite these challenges, surgical cure rates exceed 90%. Diagnosis relies on recognizing that normal PTH levels in the setting of hypercalcemia are physiologically inappropriate. [14]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Differential Diagnosis -- Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia
content: FHH is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by inactivating mutations in the CaSR gene. These mutations result in an increased calcium set point and reduced urinary calcium excretion. Clinical features include lifelong mild hypercalcemia, low urinary calcium excretion (<100 mg/24 hours), a calcium–creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01, and normal or mildly elevated PTH levels. Parathyroidectomy is ineffective and therefore not recommended. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia ," for further information. [26]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Differential Diagnosis -- Malignancy-Related Hypercalcemia
content: Malignancy is a major PTH-independent cause of hypercalcemia, affecting 20% to 30% of cancer patients. Most cases are due to the secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) by squamous cell, renal, breast, or bladder carcinomas. Other mechanisms include osteolytic metastases and cytokine-mediated bone resorption, as seen in multiple myeloma. Laboratory findings typically show elevated calcium, suppressed PTH, increased PTHrP, and normal or elevated phosphate. Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying low intact PTH and high PTHrP levels. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Malignancy-Related Hypercalcemia ," for further information. [43]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Differential Diagnosis -- Parathyroid Carcinoma
content: Parathyroid carcinoma is a rare malignancy, representing less than 1% of primary hyperparathyroidism cases. Patients typically present with markedly elevated calcium levels (>14 mg/dL) and PTH concentrations 5 to 10 times the upper normal limit, often with neck masses, hoarseness, or recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement. Clinical severity is primarily due to severe, refractory hypercalcemia rather than local tumor invasion. Histological confirmation requires evidence of capsular or vascular invasion. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Parathyroid Cancer ," for further information. [20]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Differential Diagnosis -- Parathyromatosis
content: Parathyromatosis is an uncommon cause of persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism, most frequently resulting from seeding of parathyroid tissue during surgical procedures or ablation, although it may rarely be developmental. The condition is characterized by multiple parathyroid tissue nodules embedded within fibrotic tissue, which can mimic carcinoma but lack true malignant invasion. Management is challenging; complete excision is potentially curative but technically demanding. Calcimimetics and denosumab may be used to control symptoms. [44]

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Differential Diagnosis -- Iatrogenic and Endocrine Causes
content: Lithium therapy : Lithium reduces CaSR sensitivity, increasing the calcium threshold required for PTH suppression. This may result in parathyroid hyperplasia and, over time, autonomous PTH secretion that biochemically resembles PHPT. title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis for PHPT is generally favorable, especially among patients with mild or asymptomatic disease. The severity of hypercalcemia influences long-term outcomes, the presence of complications, and the chosen treatment strategy. Most asymptomatic individuals remain stable for extended periods and have a normal life expectancy. In contrast, patients with moderate to severe hypercalcemia (serum calcium ≥10.8 mg/dL) or complications, eg, nephrolithiasis, osteoporosis, or fragility fractures, face a higher risk of morbidity and mortality. In these cases, surgical intervention substantially improves survival rates.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Prognosis
content: Parathyroidectomy achieves a cure in more than 95% of cases when performed by experienced endocrine surgeons. This procedure results in normalization of calcium and PTH levels, enhanced BMD, and decreased incidence of kidney stones and fractures. These skeletal benefits are sustained for over a decade after successful surgery. Among patients managed conservatively, most maintain stable calcium levels and BMD; however, approximately 25% to 40% experience disease progression or develop new indications for surgery within 10 to 15 years, particularly younger patients or those with higher initial calcium concentrations. In general, the long-term prognosis is excellent for patients who receive timely diagnosis, appropriate surgical intervention when indicated, and consistent monitoring of calcium levels, renal function, and bone health. title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Complications -- Complications of Untreated Primary Hyperparathyroidism
content: Complications of PHPT result from chronic hypercalcemia and excessive PTH activity, impacting the skeletal, renal, neurocognitive, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal systems. Skeletal complications are particularly significant and include progressive loss of BMD, especially at cortical sites. This loss leads to osteopenia, osteoporosis, fractures, and osteitis fibrosa cystica, which manifests as bone pain and “brown tumors.” Parathyroidectomy can reverse these skeletal effects, with BMD increasing by up to 10% within the first year and continuing to improve for more than a decade following surgery.

Surgical intervention significantly reduces the recurrence of kidney stones and helps stabilize renal function.

Chronic hypercalcemia can also cause band keratopathy and soft-tissue calcifications.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Complications -- Complications Related to Surgery
content: Although parathyroidectomy is curative in more than 95% of patients, it carries inherent surgical risks. Common postoperative complications include transient hypocalcemia, which may result from hungry bone syndrome. This syndrome is characterized by profound hypocalcemia with hypophosphatemia and elevated alkaline phosphatase following rapid skeletal remineralization. Additional complications include permanent hypoparathyroidism (1%–3%), recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (1%–2%), and, rarely, neck hematoma or persistent hyperparathyroidism due to missed multigland disease. Despite these risks, the benefits of surgery in appropriate candidates, eg, normalized calcium, improved bone and renal outcomes, and reduced long-term morbidity, outweigh the potential complications. title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Deterrence and patient education play a central role in reducing complications and disease progression associated with PHPT. Patients benefit from a clear explanation of parathyroid function and the effects of excess parathyroid hormone on calcium homeostasis, bone health, and kidney function. Education should emphasize that PHPT often causes few or no symptoms, which makes routine laboratory testing and follow-up essential even when patients feel well. Counseling on maintaining adequate hydration, avoiding excessive calcium supplementation unless prescribed, and adhering to the recommended vitamin D repletion supports stable calcium metabolism and reduces the risk of kidney stones. Patients should also understand the importance of reporting symptoms, eg, fatigue, muscle weakness, bone pain, or renal colic, promptly.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education should reinforce that parathyroidectomy offers a definitive cure for most individuals and prevents long-term skeletal and renal complications. For patients managed with observation, clinicians should stress the need for regular monitoring of serum calcium, kidney function, and bone density to detect progression early. Clear communication regarding the excellent prognosis, low surgical risk in experienced centers, and benefits of timely intervention improves shared decision-making, adherence to follow-up, and long-term outcomes, allowing most patients with PHPT to maintain healthy, normal lives.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Successful management of PHPT depends on recognizing mild or masked cases, accurately distinguishing primary from secondary causes, and selecting appropriate surgical candidates. Parathyroidectomy remains the only curative therapy. Key factors to bear in mind when managing PHPT include: Misclassification: Not correcting calcium for albumin or failing to measure ionized calcium can obscure the diagnosis. Vitamin D deficiency: Failure to replete can falsely elevate PTH and mimic PHPT. Missed cortical bone loss: Omitting distal radius DEXA can underestimate bone risk. Biotin interference: High-dose supplements can yield falsely low PTH values. Stop biotin 48 hours or more before testing. Incomplete family history: Overlooking familial syndromes (MEN, FHH) may lead to unnecessary surgery.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: PHPT is a common endocrine disorder caused by autonomous overproduction of parathyroid hormone, leading to hypercalcemia and disruption of calcium homeostasis. Most cases result from a single benign parathyroid adenoma, while multigland disease and carcinoma occur less frequently. Increased use of routine biochemical screening has shifted presentation toward asymptomatic hypercalcemia, including normocalcemic and normohormonal variants. Diagnosis relies on biochemical testing that demonstrates elevated or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone levels in the presence of hypercalcemia after secondary causes have been excluded. Parathyroidectomy provides definitive cure in most patients, while selected individuals may be managed with observation or medical therapy and structured surveillance.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective management of PHPT depends on coordinated interprofessional collaboration. Physicians and advanced practitioners oversee diagnosis and treatment by interpreting calcium and PTH levels, differentiating PHPT from secondary causes, and assessing surgical eligibility. Endocrine surgeons perform parathyroidectomy, while anesthesiologists, nurses, and perioperative staff maintain patient safety and monitor for complications such as postoperative hypocalcemia. Radiologists and nuclear medicine specialists localize affected glands. Pharmacists review medications that influence calcium balance, guide supplementation, and prevent drug interactions. Dietitians provide nutritional counseling to support appropriate calcium and vitamin D intake, and laboratory staff ensure accurate testing.
